mr president, colleagues, when assessing the italian presidency, we must not forget that the past six months were probably the most challenging from the perspective of foreign policy: from the russian aggression in ukraine to the rise of islamic state (isis) in iraq and syria, which have fundamentally altered europe’s strategic environment. under italy’s stewardship the eu responded well enough. we came together to agree on a robust sanctions package in response to russia’s blatant violation of international law, and this in itself counts as a historic achievement for our common foreign policy. in the southern neighbourhood, several eu member states, including italy, joined the international coalition against isis which halted its military advance and forced it to retreat. italy also steered the eu’s response to the immigration crisis in the mediterranean sea – the triton operation. for the moment, we should take some comfort from the fact that, in both the southern and eastern neighbourhoods, things look a little more stable than they did in the summer. we have averted the worst-case scenarios, and for that the italian presidency deserves credit.
italy has made bold plans for its presidency. priority was given to addressing youth employment through the effective implementation of the youth guarantee scheme, together with investment in education, training and labour mobility. i think that the italian presidency has not disappointed and has created the conditions for the next presidency to continue and for the creation of appropriate legislation within the eu. another very important priority was addressing the problems of asylum and migration policy in europe . we have been discussing this issue for some time, but so far no country has addressed it in the presidency. italy, as the country that receives and rescues the most migrants from countries where they are at risk of hunger, poverty and, in many cases, escape from their own country to save their health and their lives, has begun to speak very openly about the problems of asylum policy and the problems of migrants. the problem of the south of europe must be an eu problem. the creation of a common asylum and immigration policy must therefore remain a priority for the commission and all member states.
in writing i personally welcome the intention of the european commission to give member states more powers to ban the cultivation of genetically modified crops. however, it should be borne in mind that the main factor is not the existing rules but demand, which will be very hardly affected by any amendment of the legislation in the field in question. it is well known in europe that the primary reason for the low cultivation of gm crops is the lack of market demand for their supply. we cannot expect farmers to produce something that they will have a very hard time selling to their trading partners, and in practice many farmers often have customers explicitly demanding evidence that the goods they supply are not genetically modified. however, i welcome the fact that the new rules envisaged are intended to give member states greater control over the prohibition of the cultivation of this type of crop in their national agricultural sectors. however, it should also be borne in mind that countries that decide to prevent the cultivation of genetically modified organisms on their territory may face legal attack from the biotechnology industry, so it is also appropriate to put in place measures to protect them adequately.
in writing i am in favour of the proposal, as it can help to free up trade between the eu and the euro-mediterranean countries in the future. the removal of trade barriers between countries leads to greater prosperity and freedom for all involved. moreover, given that it has been more than eight years since romania and bulgaria joined the eu, it is high time that this agreement was concluded.
transport is a key element for our economy and society. it helps economic growth and job creation. since the publication of the 2001 white paper on transport, considerable progress has been made. in air, road and partly rail transport, there has been further market opening. however, the transport system is still not sustainable. its sustainability is one of the essential attributes for making it work more efficiently. as mobility is one of the important aspects of the internal market and raises the standard of living of citizens, the completion of the single transport market should be one of the eu's fundamental objectives. moreover, strong international cooperation needs to be promoted, given the global nature of transport.
the citizens of the european union, but i see that we politicians, do not have a common view on the issue of genetically modified food. on the one hand, it says that if we want to solve the world's hunger problems, we can't do without genetically modified food. the arguments against call for caution over the possible adverse effects of eating such foods. caution is in order in this situation. i therefore support the agreement reached, which will lead to a change in the current approval regime and strengthen the member states' ability to do so. under the directive in force until now, gmos were authorised centrally for the whole of the european union and national authorities had very limited options. the new legislative framework will provide more room and legal certainty for member states to ban, restrict or authorise genetically modified food.
in writing. parliament accepted the compromise that eu member states may restrict (or prohibit) the cultivation of genetically modified crops on their territory if they are otherwise authorised at eu level. under the new rules, member states can also ban the cultivation of gmos on grounds of environmental protection or agricultural policy. member states may also prohibit certain plant varieties or plants with certain characteristics. one of the main arguments for gmos is that european agriculture could become more efficient. opponents of gmos, on the other hand, warn of the risky results of production. as a biochemist, i share the view of most scientists that at this point we cannot know whether, and if so, what genetic changes are caused in the human body by foods containing genetically engineered genes. scientists also warn that it may be only in the third or fourth generation that any human genetic changes caused by gmos become apparent. the ep decided to return this power to the member states, so that each member state is free to decide whether to authorise such products or not. the technical content of the move is interesting, but also the political momentum, which the eu has taken in strengthening the competence of the member states in this matter. this will, of course, lead to complications in the future, for example in the formulation of a free trade agreement with the usa. i voted in favour of this necessary compromise.
in writing the european commission's intention to give member states more powers to ban the cultivation of genetically modified crops is a positive step. however, it should be borne in mind that the main factor is not the existing rules but demand, which will be very hardly affected by any amendment of the legislation in the field in question. it is well known in europe that the primary reason for the low cultivation of gm crops is the lack of market demand for their supply. it is impossible to expect farmers to produce something that they will have a very difficult time selling to their trading partners, and in practice it is often the case that customers explicitly require evidence that the goods supplied are not genetically modified.
i personally have a problem with the use of genetically modified organisms (gmos). but i realize that for hundreds of incurable diseases, it is only through gmos that we can develop active ingredients. the main problem concerns the exclusive cultivation of gmos for harvesting or research in the open field i. imports of gmos intended primarily for animal feed are not covered by this legislation the main objective of this amendment is to provide more room and legal certainty for member states wishing to ban the cultivation of authorised gmos in all or part of their territory. the member state concerned shall inform the commission of the results of the evaluation. the commission will be able to decide for itself whether to ban the use of the eu has some of the strictest rules in the world, and this is a very important issue for the eu. the new regulation is a further tightening of the rules. i'm in favor of compromise.
in writing in the field of genetically modified organisms, gmos, it is important that we protect the health and safety of eu citizens and member states first and foremost. the vast majority of european citizens do not want to grow and consume genetically modified crops or genetically modified animals for human consumption. today, even member states that do not expressly wish to do so have a clear right not to grow gmos on their territory. the minority of countries that already grow gmos must take measures to prevent contamination of their fields by those who grow such crops, we are talking about fields in border areas. the text adopted by the council and today by the european parliament provides for the possibility for the opt out member states not to grow gmos on their territory, which in my view increases the rights of the member states in terms of subsidiarity. there is also a safeguard clause against foreign importers, so that they cannot enforce in court the right to import such crops despite not wanting to grow them in a country. i think this text reinforces the three principles, although it's not perfect yet, it's a compromise. the three principles are transparency, health protection and safety.
in writing. the proposal we adopted, which i voted for, i regard as a step in the right direction. member states should be able to prohibit the cultivation of gmos on their territory. i'm all for subsidiarity. the result of this debate must be a better informed citizenship, since they should have the right to decide on the fate of gmos in their country. it should also be noted that the health risks associated with eating such foods are still unknown, as studies on their harmfulness are still in doubt. in order for citizens to know the truth, we need a relevant debate at the professional level, with both pro- and anti-gmo voices.
in writing - i supported the motion for a resolution to allow member states to restrict or prohibit the cultivation of gm crops for reasons other than environmental criteria. other reasons include spatial planning requirements or socio-economic reasons. i also support the introduction of 'mandatory rules' which should prevent gm crops grown in certain countries from spreading to neighbouring non-gm countries. mon810 maize is currently the only genetically modified crop grown in the european union. slovakia is a small country, growing maize on 225 thousand hectares and only 100 hectares of modified maize. the debate between those in favour and those against the cultivation of genetically modified crops will continue, but it is important that research in this area does not lag behind, that the population has all the information about the possible consequences of growing gmo crops and their subsequent inclusion in the food chain.
in writing i welcome this agreement because it will give more flexibility to member states who wish to restrict the cultivation of genetically modified crops on their territory. it is important that a scientifically based authorisation system within the eu remains in place. i also believe that a major priority in the area of gmo cultivation should be to carry out rigorous safety assessments and to strengthen the monitoring system.
in writing. the primary tasks of this committee include promoting, protecting and rationally managing living water resources, developing and recommending conservation measures and supporting cooperation projects in the field of training. at its meetings, the commission adopted measures to be incorporated into european union law on the exploitation of red coral, measures to mitigate the consequences of incidental catches of seabirds and, last but not least, measures to ensure a high level of protection from fishing activities. however, it is important to note that the gfcm proposal ignores measures already in place at national level and the european commission's proposal in this area is in many cases much stricter than the recommendations of the mediterranean fisheries commission.
in writing i support the proposal as it introduces in particular technical and other measures to increase the effectiveness of the gfcm arrangements. however, like the rapporteur, i do not agree that the commission in some cases enforces even stricter recommendations than the gfcm, even in cases where this excessive rigor is totally unjustified and contrary to scientific advice.

president-in-office of the council. - mr president, women on company boards are the next topic. the subject of the gender balance on company boards is a very important topic. there is a broad consensus in europe on the need to increase the number of women in decision-making, especially in businesses. i firmly believe that parliament, the council and the commission already agree in principle on the most crucial thing, namely that equality before the law is not enough – we also need equality in practice, and this also means ending vertical segregation. there is no reason in the 21st century why businesses, banks and the economy as a whole should be mainly run by men. allow me therefore to thank the european parliament for keeping this issue on the agenda and for insisting on progress. as the commission has also stressed, european business needs the talents of europe’s highly-educated women, and increasing diversity is also a way to improve the performance of companies. we look forward to constructive exchanges with the european parliament’s new rapporteur on this file, ms gabriel. according to the latest figures, the average share of women on boards of the largest publicly-listed companies in the eu is now 18.6%. this is a clear sign that concrete measures must be taken to remedy the situation. how do we ensure that our largest companies can benefit from the talents and dynamism of both women and men? it is a generally political question and policymakers have divergent views on approaches and what tools we should use. we should therefore not be surprised if more time is needed to agree. the goal we share can be reached by different roads. as you know, some member states have already introduced binding quotas. others are wary of interfering with company law and prefer self-regulatory measures. by means of example, the share of women on the boards of latvia’s largest companies is 31%. i am proud to say that this result has been achieved without any formal measures of positive discrimination. how do we crack the glass ceiling? what is the eu’s proper role in this? the commission’s proposal for a directive in this area seeks to answer the question in its own way. the proposal itself is a compromise of sorts. it does not provide for binding quotas. instead, it sets quantitative objectives. the main obligations that the proposal contains concern the procedure for selecting board members, which should be fair, merit-based and transparent. i note that the european parliament already adopted its first reading position on the commission’s proposal in late 2013. in that opinion your institution broadly endorsed the approach suggested by the commission. it is no secret that the negotiations on the council side have been challenging. despite efforts made by successive presidencies, our discussions have not yet been completed. views still differ between the member states regarding the best approach. the diversity between member states needs to be respected in term of company law, the degree of gender balance already achieved and the national measures already taken to improve it. the member states are taking action but in different ways. we must also remember that the member states start from very different levels. one thing is becoming clear: from the subsidiarity perspective, any future measures at european level should recognise the fact that there is no one-size-fits-all solution. this was the spirit of the approach taken by the italian presidency. building on this work, we will continue our search for a solution under the latvian presidency. on behalf of the council i assure you that we will take forward this work with a view to reaching an agreement.
member of the commission. - mr president, honourable members, i would like first to thank you for adding this item to the agenda because it gives me an opportunity to present here the clear position of the commission, and of myself, on this important piece of legislation which is – hopefully – in the process of adoption. we are fully aware that major steps on the road to effective gender equality need to be taken. the adoption of the directive on improving gender balance on company boards will be an important step on that road. the directive will help smash the glass ceiling that prevents qualified women from holding top jobs. the directive is smart and flexible: it puts qualification and merit centre stage. this european union instrument is as necessary as ever. on boards of private companies we still have only 18% women. at the same time, 60% of new university graduates in europe are female. their talent should not be wasted, in particular in light of the demographic changes we face in europe. it is well recognised in numerous studies that a range of talents, experience and skills in the boardroom improves business performance and governance and drives economic growth. if we want to maintain europe’s competitiveness and stay ahead of demographic changes, we need more women at work, especially qualified women. some member states have seen positive developments, mainly those such as france, belgium and italy that have introduced, or are considering, legally binding measures. however, in others the situation is stagnating or even worsening. we have tried non-legislative action at eu level, but with limited results as you all know. only a legally binding measure at eu level can effectively contribute to greater gender equality in the area of economic decision-making. we will therefore intensify our efforts to speed up the process of the adoption of this directive. let me remind you that what the directive seeks is progress and fairness. we do not want women to be privileged because they are women. we want qualified women to get a fair chance. this is why, rather than imposing a particular result, the proposed directive requires member states to ensure that qualification, competence and professional performance play the key role during the process of selection to board positions. this approach is in line with the case law of the court of justice, which has set rules and conditions for positive action for the under-represented sex in employment. it requires a comparative assessment of all candidates on the basis of objective criteria. since there are highly qualified women capable of being selected as candidates, this approach is the right one to take. i see that considerable efforts have been made by previous presidencies; this is very welcome and there are concrete results from these efforts. the proposal is moving closer to achieving a qualified majority in the council. in particular, the italian presidency has worked intensively on this directive and i am convinced that, on this solid basis, it is possible to agree that subsidiarity concerns be fully addressed. this should ensure the support of a sufficient majority of member states. latvia is among the member states which have recently adopted a more positive approach to the directive. the commission is therefore encouraging the latvian presidency to use this positive momentum, actively to pursue the discussion and then to reach a compromise solution.
for the ecr group the natural desire of every human is to realize his potential. as a mother of three who has been active in politics for several years, i believe that whether a woman decides to devote her life purely to her family or to combine family and work, it is our duty to create the right conditions for her to do so. unfortunately, the proposal which provides for quotas for the representation of women on the supervisory boards of companies does not create such conditions. this is clearly demonstrated by the example of norway, where quotas were introduced in 2006 but did not have the desired effect. the norwegian employers' representatives agreed that a sufficient number of places in kindergartens and well-established parental leave are much more crucial not only for women's performance in top positions but also for their overall participation in the labour market. the european commission itself, as well as some member states, is an example of good practice in the field of parental leave, where employees can take part of this leave flexibly up to the age of 12. i was inspired by this amendment and am currently trying to push it through the slovak parliament. i believe that this way i can make a much more meaningful contribution to enabling women to realize their potential and not be bogged down by the question: work or family?
in writing. the terrorist attack in paris is further sad evidence that internal security in the eu requires careful reassessment and significant reinforcement. concerns about internal security in the context of the fight against organised crime, terrorism and violent extremism are also closely linked to the persistence of economic repression and political developments in the eu's neighbourhood, where many criminal activities originate or are organised. our society must be able to deal comprehensively with security threats whose dimensions and sophistication are constantly growing. in a globalised world, crime ignores borders and it is no longer within the power of individual member states to tackle these threats on their own. solidarity and cooperation are the keys to success. we must act together to achieve the level of security that eu citizens deserve and that they expect from us as public officials.
corruption is a phenomenon with enormous negative economic and social consequences, and we must therefore constantly draw attention to its harmfulness and take measures to reduce the incentive and scope for corrupt behaviour by public officials. corruption drains scarce public resources from the areas where they should be spent, prevents improvements (or causes deterioration) in the quality and availability of public services, and hinders economic growth. corruption also negatively affects good governance and contributes to the erosion of trust in public institutions and democratic processes. the slovak republic is among the countries with the highest perceived corruption rates in the eu (cpi, corruption perceptions index according to transparency international), but at least in the legislative field, it has made significant progress in reducing the space for corrupt behaviour over the last decade. examples include the reform of the trade register, the increase in the share of eligible permits and licences, or the recent passing of a law that significantly increases the incentive to report corrupt behaviour, both by providing more effective protection for the whistleblower against possible sanctions by the employer, and by offering the possibility of receiving financial rewards for reporting corruption. more than shortcomings in anti-corruption legislation, the current problem in the fight against corruption in slovakia is very weak enforcement of the law, which is related to the long-term state of justice.

member of the commission. - madam president, i will do my introduction in english and will give my answers as usual in dutch. allow me to present to you a proposal which the commission adopted last wednesday on youth employment. since i came to office as the new commissioner for employment, social affairs, skills and labour mobility, i have made the fight against youth unemployment my first priority. more than five million young people in europe do not have a job at this moment. this is around one in five of young people in europe. in some member states we are facing youth unemployment rates of around 50%. moreover, today 7.5 million people between 15 and 24 years old are not in employment, education or training and risk being socially and economically excluded, with all the dramatic consequences for themselves and for our society. this is unacceptable. this is why, in its work programme for 2015, the commission committed to taking initiatives to promote integration and employability in the labour market, including measures to support member states in getting young people into work. as you know, the youth employment initiative was established following the urgent call from the european council in february 2013 to address the unprecedented levels of youth unemployment in certain regions of the european union most affected by this phenomenon. this budget line of eur 3.2 billion, to be matched with funding from the european social fund, is dedicated to actions targeting individual young people who are neither in employment, education or training. therefore, it contributes to the implementation of the youth employment guarantee, in line with the council’s recommendation of 22 april 2013. however, despite the provisions already in place to frontload this initiative, and an early eligibility date for expenditure – 1 september 2013 – progress has not yet lived up to expectations. the initial pre-financing amount of 1% – and 1.5% in the member states in the programme – proved to be too low to roll out the initiative, particularly to those member states that have significant budgetary constraints. this proposal aims, therefore, to tackle this deficiency by setting an adequate level of pre-financing for the youth employment initiative. the increased financing proposed will amount to around eur 1 billion – 30% of the specific allocation – instead of the current eur 39 million. based on the targets set by member states in their operational programmes, we expect that, with this additional pre-financing, up to 650 000 young people will be able to rapidly receive support. i would like to underline again that the pre-financing proposal does not impact on the budgetary allocations for the youth employment initiative in 2015, or the multiannual financial framework overall. neither does it affect pre-financing payments from other funds or under operational programmes that are not relevant for the initiative. the urgency to adopt this proposal is justified by the figures. the longer we wait to act, the harder it becomes to help the young generation. i would like, therefore, to ask you to join me in the effort to make this proposal a reality for young people and to ensure that this additional funding can be converted as soon as possible into a concrete job, education or training offer for young people. (applause)
for the ecr group it is good news that the commission has decided to focus on young people. we know the amazing things our young people can do when given the opportunity, but we also know how much entire nations can suffer if young people are not given the opportunity to develop their work potential in time. the aim of the guarantee is to ensure that young people do not remain inactive for more than four months and get a job, a traineeship or further education. the funds are now being released for this purpose and the instruction is: expedite implementation. but do member states have the capacity to use them meaningfully? sadly, the answer to that question is not clear. i understand if the commission needs to show that it is proactive and quick, but my concerns about the unwise use of accelerated payments remain. the programme is in danger of going the easy way: by pointlessly subsidising the rapid creation of, unfortunately, often temporary jobs. the problem of unemployment does not begin at the employment office, but much, much earlier. for example, when a child from a bad social environment doesn't get into kindergarten, when a child does get into school, but for years he learns old and unusable theory. when college doesn't even know about working with real business. and then, in the worst case, graduates end up in the office working and meeting people who don't know how to help them. for example, did you know that in slovakia there are sometimes up to 700 unemployed people for every civil servant? so if the commission today is proud of the speed of its work, i am more concerned about dishonesty. i think it is unfair that employment is being tackled in the regions with the greatest problems too quickly, with questionable implementation capacities. i think it is equally questionable to pour money into often helpless states to subsidize jobs. i understand the commission's intention, but i'm concerned about the outcome in reality. so i'm gonna be very careful with my colleagues setting up the control system. to pour money into a broken system without structural change would be a disappointment to all of us.
to think that with one billion euros you can create hundreds of thousands of jobs is a pure illusion. you probably don't believe that yourself. the commission promised new beginnings, and yet you can only do the same thing over and over again. you just keep putting more and more money into more and more programs. this doesn't work, but look at the bad situation today. politicians can't create jobs. politicians can only create the conditions for job creation. therefore, the only solution is to reduce the regulatory burden. the european union is the most regulated economic area in the world. there's the problem. not whether you give a billion or two or ten. we've been through all that. you have to improve the business environment, and in doing so, you also save a lot of money that can be left to entrepreneurs. they know best.

in writing. i am fully aware of the gravity of the situation in ukraine and support all efforts to find a peaceful solution, including eu sanctions against russia. i also condemn the annexation of crimea as a step that was contrary to international law. but i fundamentally disagree with all the european union's efforts to provide financial assistance to ukraine so far. the reason for the bad economic situation in ukraine is not the conflict with russia, but the long-term neglect of reforms and corruption by all ukrainian governments over the past 20 years. the european union's loans cannot solve this situation, but only real reforms that will lead to greater competitiveness of ukraine. the international monetary fund, which has been far more successful than the european union in rescuing troubled countries, should therefore continue to play this role.
when i received a book called the flower of the desert by waris dirie years ago, i must admit that i was shocked. i had never heard of female circumcision. her autobiographical account only increased my horror. it was not fiction, but a harsh reality. and that reality persists to this day. even today, hundreds of thousands of girls, both young and old, are subjected to this barbaric and unprecedented procedure every year. and besides some ritual practice, it has no religious basis and is not a medically approved procedure. quite the opposite. many girls bleed to death during the procedure, while others suffer daily pain for the rest of their lives. they're struggling not only with inflammation, but with indescribable pain from ordinary urination or menstruation. but the scars remain not only on the body but also on the soul. it is therefore our duty to condemn this ritual mutilation and to call on other african countries to follow the example of ethiopia and côte d'ivoire by banning female circumcision by law, with severe punishment for the perpetrators. since, unfortunately, these practices are also occurring in europe, we must do everything possible to prevent such procedures from taking place in our countries and to punish not only those who carry them out but also the parents who allow their daughter to be mutilated.
the mutilation of the human body is reprehensible. and while i have great respect for a person's religious feelings and beliefs, i must emphasize that it is not mandated by any of the world's religions, including islam. i cannot recall exactly how many times we have discussed this subject in the european parliament over the last ten years. we held conferences and passed resolutions. but this debate has shown that we have not gone far. my opposition to female circumcision is very strong. i support all the tools and policies that will increase prevention while affecting everyone involved in the effort. but i do not agree that the effort to end this barbaric practice should be used as a pretext to press for the accelerated ratification of the 2010 istanbul convention. this is entirely a matter for the member states and the commission has no right to put any pressure on them in this respect.

in writing the subject of international child abduction largely concerns spouses or couples in which individuals from different countries around the world decide to take advantage of the situation by illegally adopting a child after a divorce or separation. such situations are helped by the hague convention on the civil aspects of international child abduction. children often become a means of settling scores between spouses or former partners of different nationalities. the courts of individual countries, often outside the european union, often subsequently, due to certain national tendencies, grant custody to a parent who is a citizen of the country to which the court belongs. the convention deals with such situations in such a way that the court of the state of the child's habitual residence decides on the child's allocation, irrespective of where one of the parents has been taken. the eu now has exclusive external competence in this area, as confirmed by the court of justice. this means that member states no longer act on their own discretion. it is therefore necessary to adopt a council decision requiring the member states to accept, on their own territory, the accession of gabon to the convention and, consequently, the effective entry into force of the convention between the european union and that state. the adoption of the convention will ensure increased protection for children who are in any way connected with the gabonese community.
in writing i welcome the accession of gabon to the hague convention. children who are connected in some way to the gabonese community will thus be protected from abduction. any initiative that succeeds in widening the number of countries acceding to the 1980 hague convention on the civil aspects of international child abduction should be supported. this will increase the protection of children in the event of abduction on the territory of the contracting states and may thus help to speed up the return of the child to his or her natural environment. it is therefore necessary to seek the most effective ways of addressing international child abduction in order to protect children and strengthen their rights.
in writing. these reports, however technical, draw attention to a situation that is becoming more and more topical. all statistics show that marriages are breaking up more and more frequently around the world. and the direct consequence of that is that children are being beaten up. of course, the accession of these countries to the hague convention is welcome, since the most important thing in such cases is that the child is placed as soon as possible in a stable, peaceful, loving environment. as europeans committed to our fundamental values, including the rights of the child, we can also see these accessions as a reminder to always have the best interests of the child at heart in our procedural law and practice. i therefore urge that, at least in the relations between the eu member states, we go beyond the standards of the international convention. minimize the administrative burden of the procedure, avoid using language requirements to delay the procedure and ensure that it is carried out quickly and carefully.
in writing - it is essential that the provisions of this convention on preventing and preventing international child abduction apply also to other countries which have not yet committed themselves to it or have only acceded to it. that's why i voted yes. it should be stressed that even in these very complex family law situations, often with a strong geopolitical context, where national courts tend to make decisions in an unbiased manner, it is always necessary to take account of the rights, welfare and dignity of children at all costs. the child may not be abused in any way and may not be subjected to emotional, psychological or physical suffering. and not even in a situation where an adult is trying to claim a so-called 'right to a child'. the child is not a commodity to be used as a commodity or a tool for the exploitation of others, as is often the case in these cases. the best interests of the child must always and everywhere come first.

the european union must find a way to punish those drivers who take vehicles beyond the borders of their home country, thus contributing to reducing road fatalities. we must send a clear signal to the citizens of the european union that everyone will be treated equally, regardless of where their vehicle is registered. the amendment of the legal basis of the directive makes it possible to extend the application of the new rules to ireland, denmark and the united kingdom, which were not covered by the original directive.
in writing the purpose of the directive is to improve road safety. the scope of the directive had to be amended to take road safety as its legal basis, but also to extend it to apply to all member states to which it had not previously applied. studies have shown, for example, that most of the persons concerned who exceeded the speed limit were foreigners. a typical example is austria. the competent authorities did not know the residence of the vehicle owner and the recovery of fines, in particular from automatic radars, was problematic. this relative impunity has had a negative impact on the growth of offences and accidents. road traffic rules needed to be harmonized. these rules have already had the effect of reducing accidents by 40%. therefore, it was necessary to remove all irregularities and extend it to the whole eu territory without exception.
in writing i consider the current situation, where, except for direct police control, drivers cannot be punished for road traffic offences committed in another eu country, to be unfair and therefore supported the proposal. i am convinced that drivers should always be punished equally for the same traffic offences, regardless of the country in which their motor vehicle is registered in the european union.
in writing today, with the majority of meps, i voted in favour of a report which aims to make it impossible for drivers who break road rules outside their home eu country to escape fines. i welcome the commission's swift response to the court of justice's judgment that the original 2011 directive had an incorrect legal basis. the long-standing legal vacuum in this area would be unnecessary given the good wording of the original text. the directive has changed in only two ways. in addition to the legal basis mentioned above (changing from police cooperation to transport safety), its territorial scope has been extended to denmark, the united kingdom and ireland, which had previously enjoyed an exemption.

in writing. - parliament drew conclusions from the scandal of beef and veal mixed with horse meat and asked the commission to submit a legislative proposal to clearly specify the indication of the origin of meat on all products. the ep also called for the commission to present a new version of the rules, which would make it compulsory to indicate the place of birth, rearing and slaughter, and remove the exceptions for offal and minced meat. we have adopted a resolution as a result of the work. the new legislation will become mandatory from april 2015. several expressed concern that mandatory labelling could not only lead to price increases for food business operators, but also lead to higher consumer prices. i think that none of these aspects can be ignored, but we cannot expose consumers to health or food safety risks. the balance between the two sides is the most important for the union market. the european parliament argues that the new rules have the advantage of allowing the origin of meat ingredients to be indicated, which would help to better monitor the ingredients and also make it easier for producers to choose between suppliers and products. i voted in favour of the rapporteur's proposals.
european consumers have the right to be protected to the greatest possible extent and to be adequately informed about the origin of meat in all processed foods. the european commission should submit proposals as soon as possible to introduce mandatory indication of the country of production, slaughter and processing for all meat in already processed food and not just for fresh meat. as many as 90% of consumers would clearly welcome the extension of the mandatory origin labelling rules in question to meat contained in ready-to-eat foods such as baguettes, sandwiches or various types of semi-finished products. the measure in question would clearly help people to better orient themselves when buying and selecting such products. if something is labeled as a slovak product, it should mean that the meat in it also comes from slovakia. with today's rules, it may not be taken for granted. transparent labelling should lead to a deepening of consumer confidence, which has unfortunately been marred by several scandals in the past, and should contribute to improving the quality of food, to a certain extent also its safety and, above all, consumer information.
in writing maximising consumer awareness of the composition of food and food products is also a way to improve the health of the population. the consumer has the right to decide what food to buy, not only in terms of price, but also in terms of its composition, origin and health. we live in a time when allergies of various kinds are becoming a part of our lives. accurate labelling of food is one way to improve the health of the population. recently, we have witnessed unfair manipulation of the provenance of meat in processed foods. it is therefore essential that the commission submits legislative proposals urgently to address the origin identification of individual ingredients in processed foods in order to prevent fraud in the nutrition of the population and to strengthen consumer protection.
in writing mandatory country of origin labelling for meat used in processed foods is, in my view, the only rational way to ensure greater transparency throughout the food chain and to improve the information of european consumers, whose confidence has been shaken by the horse and other meat scandals of recent years. i therefore voted in favour of the resolution calling on the european commission to submit an appropriate legislative proposal introducing mandatory country of origin labelling for meat in the eu, taking into account sanitary safety, product quality, but also the needs of small and medium-sized enterprises in the regions.
in writing. — i think it is important for each consumer to know the composition and origin of the food they consume. this will contribute to greater public awareness and also to better decision-making for better and healthier food.
in writing it is important to guarantee the safety and improved quality of food for our consumers. this is ensured by the harmonisation of the food and hygiene legislation of the member states. there is therefore no link between the introduction of the indication of the country of origin of processed meat and the subsequent improvement of its quality. the opinion of consumers should also be taken into account, where up to 80% expressed that they were not interested in labelling if it increased the price. mandatory labelling of processed meat will not only affect our consumers, who will be charged higher prices for the products they buy, but also small and medium-sized enterprises, which represent up to 90% of meat processors in the eu, which will be charged up to 30% more in administrative costs. in this way, we will not only lower the standard of living of our citizens, but also lower the level of employment and threaten the existence of smes in the eu and in the slovak republic. mandatory labelling would limit the variability of goods offered, especially for smes, where up to 90% of goods are sold unpackaged. the introduction of simple and flexible labelling rules and voluntary labelling in meat products, which is also called for by the meat processing associations concerned, can be a starting point. at the same time, the introduction of mandatory labelling could lead to an increase in the illegal sale of products and would not guarantee the 100% accuracy of the data provided, given that back-checking is burdensome, that not only increase the costs of producers, but also exceed the capabilities of the current level of control bodies.
in writing despite the improvement of food control systems, the tightening of measures and the increase in sanctions, food scandals are on the increase. on the one hand, consumers today have access to a wide variety of products, but on the other hand, they are faced with food that is of poor quality and may even pose a serious threat to their health. in order to better orient buyers on the market, it is important that the description of the products includes not only the content but also the origin of the food. according to consumer surveys from 2013, more than 90% of respondents indicated that the origin of meat used in processed foods should be indicated on the packaging in order to be able to make a decision also on the basis of this information. therefore, in the interest of consumer protection, i agree that in the foreseeable future, meat used as an ingredient in processed foods such as lasagne, ravioli, etc. will be subject to rules of origin identical to those applicable to fresh beef. although i am not in favour of excessive regulation, i support this proposal because i believe that consumers have a right to access to clear labelling of all food ingredients.

in writing ‒ consumers are generally unaware of the fees charged by merchants for the payment instrument they use. various incentive practices applied by issuers (such as travel vouchers, bonuses, rebates, reverse transactions, free insurance, etc.) can drive consumers to use payment instruments and thus generate high fee income. this must be prevented. there is a need for a clearly defined ceiling for the fees that banks charge retailers for processing card payments across the eu. both cross-border and domestic card payments will be subject to limits. this will reduce costs for merchants as well as for cardholders themselves.
in writing ‒ payment cards have gained wide acceptance among all age groups of consumers across the eu over the last decade and are the most commonly used electronic payment instrument for purchases. however, the payment card market in the union is not yet sufficiently integrated as there are many national barriers to many payment solutions and their providers, including barriers to entry. in my view, the same rules for payments should be established across the eu, which will not only provide clarity to consumers and businesses but also lead to more dynamic competition in the internal market. since it is in my interest to facilitate the efficient functioning of the internal market and to simplify the use of electronic payments for the benefit of traders and consumers, i voted in favour of adopting this report.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the cap on interbank fees at 0.2% for debit payments and 0.3% for credit payments. internet payments are becoming cheaper and safer for retailers and consumers alike. the imposition of excessive prices and, more importantly, the misleading of consumers will be brought to an end. in addition, we will provide a level playing field for payment service providers, which will help new players to enter the market. i think the regulation goes beyond itself, because i hope it will encourage innovation. the introduction of new mobile and internet payment solutions would also improve the eu's competitiveness.
in writing ‒ i voted for the regulation. it should be noted, however, that the proposal to set a ceiling on fees aims to achieve a reduction in fees, but in practice it may achieve the opposite. several similar experiments in the past have not shown a direct profit for the consumer. the exact opposite can result an increase in fees. this is a good intention, but eu regulation often goes beyond the stated effort.
in writing i supported the legislative proposal that we have set that the fees that banks charge retailers for processing card payments will have a defined ceiling throughout the eu. the limits, which will apply to both cross-border and domestic card payments, will reduce costs for both merchants and cardholders. this legislation, together with the future payment services directive, will create uniform rules for payments across europe. it will contribute to greater transparency of charges, promote competition and allow retailers and users to choose the payment card scheme that offers them the best terms. payment cards are currently the most commonly used electronic payment instrument for retail purchases, and therefore secure, efficient, competitive and innovative electronic payments are essential if consumers, merchants and companies are to reap the full benefits of the internal market, especially as the world increasingly uses electronic commerce.

in writing. ‒ i am pleased that the joint resolution on sexual abuse of children online includes some of the wording that i introduced. the online presentation of child sexual abuse is a serious crime that requires a comprehensive approach. this should include effective detection of crime, prosecution of perpetrators, protection of child victims and measures to prevent the phenomenon. it is essential that the offenders are subject to effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties. the internet is becoming more widely available, but it also poses more and more dangers that many minors are unaware of. since images and videos can be shared long after the sexual abuse has occurred and can remain freely available to anyone on the internet, victims are constantly at risk of being victimized and stigmatized again. the darknet also deserves special attention, as it presents specific challenges. i consider it important that existing eu legislation, in particular directive 2011/93/eu on combating sexual abuse of children, is transposed into the national legal order of all member states without delay. a coordinated european approach is needed. in order to act effectively, it is essential that member states take seriously the commitments they have made in european and international fora and do everything possible to protect children. that is why i voted in favour of the report.

in writing the 2013 annual report on human rights and democracy in the world is a landmark document that sets out the way forward in the field of human rights on the basis of its findings. it is important to work continuously on an effective system of human rights monitoring throughout the european union. at the same time, a policy of establishing and respecting human rights and democracy by all eu institutions and bodies and by the member states should be promoted internationally.
in writing ‒ the report on human rights and democracy in the world deals with areas where the union and therefore the european parliament have no competence under the founding treaties. this concerns in particular the regulation of abortion and family law, including the recognition or non-recognition of so-called same-sex marriages, which are a matter for the member states. in this respect, i would like to remind this house that no international human rights instrument, nor eu law, recognises the right to terminate a pregnancy as a human right. however, it should be stressed that the eu charter of fundamental rights clearly enshrines 'everyone's right to life' and that this right is one that the eu institutions, including the ep, are obliged not only to respect but also to protect and promote in their recommendations. i therefore find it unacceptable that the ep's owninitiative reports periodically contain language which encourages easy access to contraception and abortion or condemns or criticises member states for exercising their contractual rights in the area of family law. for the reasons i have given, i voted against all the amendments in that spirit.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the report and am very pleased that it recognises the need to review the human rights clauses in the international treaties signed by the european union with third countries, in particular with regard to china and russia. we must make it clear that the success of international relations is threatened by gross violations of human rights, which affect economic, social and political life. it is time that human rights become an integral part of our international relations and treaties and all our political action. let the european union be an example for third countries. but to do that, we have to keep our own front door clean. it is unacceptable that we should be raising the issue of the fundamental human right to a fair trial, for example, with third countries, while in slovakia, an eu member state, the state is pursuing a concept lawsuit against its own citizen in the case of malina hedvig. and he's doing this because he can't face the fact that the student was actually beaten up on the street in 2006 because she spoke in her native language, hungarian. it's time to end the double standard. it's time to face our own demons back home.
i consider the 2013 report on human rights and democracy in the world and the eu's policy on the matter to be very important. even in the 21st century, respect for human rights is not taken for granted in europe and the world. still, nationality, race, gender, or religious affiliation are grounds for violations of human dignity and rights. but poverty and social exclusion, which lower living standards, are also the cause of the failure to implement the universal declaration of human rights. respect for human rights, including economic, cultural, social and environmental rights, access to food, peace, security and access to a fair and effective judiciary, is a fundamental prerequisite for reducing poverty and inequality in individual member states, but also in the world. the eu supports many countries, many development programmes, so financial and development support should also be conditional on respect for fundamental human rights.
written ‒ i abstained from voting on the report because, although it makes many recommendations and findings in the fight against human rights violations, it also goes far beyond its mandate and the human rights field in many other cases. the report also intends to influence areas such as fiscal policy, migration, climate policy, asylum and migration policy, and so on.
in writing ‒ in the context of the report on the observance of human rights and democracy in the world, i was responsible for the preparation of the opinion on women's rights and gender equality. in my opinion, i pointed out that domestic violence is one of the most widespread violations of human rights ever. i stressed that the key to tackling this problem is to train experts (health workers, police officers, prosecutors and judges) to provide adequate help and support to victims of violence. and we also need to work with young people in particular to teach us as a society that bruises and slaps are not something that we can accept as normal. in my opinion, i also point to the need to pay specific attention to women and children in war conflicts and humanitarian crises, underline the need to improve the life chances of roma women and the importance of promoting the principles of inclusive education. since the report also included issues (sexual and reproductive rights) which, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, fall within the competence of the member states, i could not support the report and abstained.

‒ the silver moron is a noble species of fish that is highly sought after by the fishing industry for its significant high value. the international council for the exploration of the sea distinguishes between four species of silver moray and several studies have shown that the decline in the population is worrying. national fisheries management measures are not sufficient to conserve this species and do not address the problem of sharing and access to resources. i therefore support the adoption of european management measures and the establishment of a multiannual management plan to ensure that the silver moray population exceeds the maximum sustainable yield.

i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. in 1970 one german mark cost nine drachmas. thirty years later, in 2000, one deutsche mark was worth 170 drachmas. this exchange rate development reflects the development of competitiveness. if the eurozone did not exist, one deutsche mark would cost 250 drachmas today. but no, the creators of the eurozone have said that the ratio is fixed for all eternity: one german mark costs 176 drachmas! that is why the euro is too cheap for germany and too expensive for greece. and that's why greece has no chance of surviving in the eurozone. i therefore support mr lucke's motion. what we need is a system for exiting the eurozone.

tax policy has long been a familiar subject in the european union. it has always been postponed and always been postponed because of some fear and concern about tax harmonization. it's been ringing off the hook a few times today. but it must be said frankly that tax harmonization should be the icing on the cake and at this point it should be preceded by very strong and clear measures to prevent tax evasion, but also to prevent companies within the european union from always being able to look for the country with the preferential rate for their business activities. an example of this is health insurance in slovakia. the law requires every citizen of the slovak republic to pay for health insurance, and some companies are domiciled in other member states of the european union, where the rate is much more favorable for providing this service. that is why tax policy is very important, because it protects our employees and it protects people in the member states.

for the ecr group. the minimum wage is economic nonsense in itself because it affects the most vulnerable, those whose skills are valued below the minimum wage. these employees are effectively prohibited from working. it is clearer than the sun that the minimum wage increases unemployment, especially if it is set as high as the german one. germany has probably forgotten that 10 years ago it was the sick man of europe, but if germany decides to harm its economy, that is its problem and its business. but germany is abusing the minimum wage to improperly close its market: this is contrary to the single free market. the minimum wage law is discriminatory in that it unfairly burdens only foreign hauliers with excessive administration, not domestic hauliers who do not have these obligations. in addition, the allowances must not be part of the minimum wage, which means that in the end the foreign carrier has to pay more than the german one - this is another discrimination. this is wrong, especially from a country that has strong exports because it benefits from a weak euro at the expense of economically weaker countries. i therefore ask the european commission to act decisively in this case and to force germany to limit its minimum wage to only employment relationships subject to german law. this means that for hauliers, the minimum wage applies to the haulage, but not to transport, export or import.
in writing. the german minimum wage law is problematic and has therefore sparked a passionate debate at european level. it is directly related to the principle of the free movement of services and restores national protectionism. it severely restricts slovak freight forwarding companies. the situation is serious and i consider it to be contrary to the principle of free markets and the free movement of goods within the eu. this principle is part of the eu's fundamental freedoms. that is why i support the idea of abolishing the law in road transport in germany.
in writing. the institution of a minimum wage in each state is a measure that social democrats can only support. on the other hand, it is inadmissible that this interferes with the laws of other countries which regulate the level of the minimum wage. on the one hand, it is understandable that germany should require sufficient financial security for persons employees moving within its territory. on the other hand, germany thus interferes with the laws of other countries, which has further effects, for example on the complexity of payroll accounting (recording of work journeys, tracking of border crossing times). this complicates labour relations (and thus wage claims) between employees and employers based in another country. germany's move is discriminatory, especially in relation to the new member states, and creates a situation of unequal treatment where operators from these states are unable to cover the costs of the measure and can therefore be forced out of the german market. in any case, the situation requires a comprehensive solution. the commission must therefore continue to act to ensure that the european treaties are not violated.
in writing. the german minimum wage law is contrary to the principle of the single market. it also infringes the eu principle of the free movement of services. this is a disadvantage for businesses in 16 eu member states and, if allowed to remain so, could create a domino effect, effectively destroying the single market. today, a german truck driver earns 8.5 euros an hour. a slovakian gets 2.5 euros for the same work. it would be nice if slovak workers were also paid german wages, although we would be there, but if we think a little realistically, we can see that the real purpose of the german provision is to help german workers. slovak entrepreneurs will simply lose their competitiveness under such conditions, and this means, in black and white, job insecurity. the european commission, as the guardian of eu law, has a duty to ensure that member states' laws do not conflict with the eu acquis. i trust the outgoing hoof will get caught in the commission's fiber.
in writing. the german legislation is a precedent in that it introduces a wage for employees from other countries. it is essential to uphold the principles of free movement in our common european market and not to create barriers between the east and the west of the eu. i call on the european commission to act immediately in this case.

vice-president of the commission.– madam president, thank you for bringing this topic for discussion here in this chamber. for the commission, the whole question of having a diverse staff, of being inclusive, has a very high priority, and i can confirm that in my first meetings with mr juncker that was a topic he brought up, specifically in regard to people with disabilities. we are very keen to address this at three levels: at the level of recruitment, at the level of inclusion in the staff of the institutions, and also in terms of the support that is being provided, as needs might change. we have a general principle of non-discrimination on various grounds in our staff regulations, amongst them disabilities, and our commitment to everybody, to each and every one of our staff, is that of fair treatment and equal opportunities. so let me stress, as we are having this discussion, that it comes at a very opportune moment for us because we are working on a new diversity strategy for the period 2015-2019, and in this sense input from the members of this parliament would be very useful. let me first start with the recruitment phase. we take very seriously our ability to provide conditions for each and every person in europe who wants to apply for a job in the european union institutions to be able to do so. we have in our team dealing with recruitment, in epso, two experts specifically for the issue of disabilities. in their work they are able to inform candidates and then respond to requests for special accommodation for testing; for example, tests in braille, on paper, with extra time. to be assessed in special facilities we have three rooms that are specifically for people with physical disabilities and, where this is appropriate, an individual person would be assigned to assist the candidate in the application. each file is then processed individually to ensure the best possible match between the needs of the candidate and the principles of both proportionality and equal treatment. secondly, in terms of being able to accommodate people with disabilities in commission buildings, we have accessibility in all our buildings and they comply with the recommendations on accessibility by people with physical disabilities that are applicable in the region of brussels. i would also say that we are looking at whether we can strive towards adopting best practices from elsewhere, at what is being done in other places. thirdly, in human resources there is a platform to provide advice and support – for example, for the need to have ergonomically better conditions for work. we are not able to provide a full file on people with disabilities because of respect for confidentiality in medical records, but that does not mean that we are not making every effort possible to be aware of whom they are and where they are. i can tell you that we use the staff survey. we used it this year and last year to give people a chance to identify themselves through the staff survey, and on that basis we know that 5.7 % this year, 2014, have identified themselves as people with disabilities. this is one percentage more than in last year’s survey. this does not mean a one-to-one match, but it gives us an indication that our efforts to recruit more people with disabilities seem to be bearing fruit. parliament asks whether it would not be more appropriate to apply quotas. our current staff regulations do not allow for quotas, but they do encourage us to use other ways to enhance diversity and i can say on my own behalf, and on behalf of my team, that we are looking for ways in which we can do more so that those of us in the commission, in parliament, in the council, those who work in the institutions can be a mirror image of what europe is, who we europeans are. we are not there yet, so we have work to do, and i look forward to the debate this evening to give us input in that direction.
for the ecr group breaking down barriers is extremely important, and i always welcome the fact that the issue of the employment of people with disabilities is not only talked about but also acted upon. the european union, as a signatory to the convention on the rights of persons with disabilities, and its institutions should clearly set an example for the member states, and it is a good idea to clean up, so to speak, at one's own doorstep. i understand that quotas can be an attractive solution, but i think it's much more important to create conditions that are responsive to the needs of people with disabilities. we should strive to make accessibility a natural and automatic process, one that the european institutions do not forget when building buildings, marking rooms, providing interpreters, creating their materials and websites or providing other support services. these are all areas in which the european parliament itself is still, unfortunately, too lacking. for any of us can become disabled from day to day. he'll lose his sight, he'll lose his hearing, he'll end up in a wheelchair, or he'll end up with a chronic disease, and so thinking in the spirit of universal design and barrier-free thinking should be taken for granted, even without quotas.
i, my colleagues, have a very different view: no quotas. what do you want to pick them on, the disabled people? different disabled people have different requirements for aids for a particular job. for example, blind, deaf, mute, handicapped people will need increased adaptation costs for specific jobs. i would suggest something else. better to create a program to support sheltered workshops, production cooperatives, better to support and facilitate employers for such projects and more to control the functioning of those projects so that the money is not misused. i know from slovakia that they were abused like this. plus, we'll create a public awareness and education program to help integrate them and facilitate the use of their employment, talents and skills. you see, i had a disabled son, and he had a good education in what is called family school, so i say that the european institutions should be encouraged to create quality, specialised fields of study for their personal growth, to find good jobs, to start with the youth, education and in a few years they will be well employed. those who do well will be skilled. so, mrs. kozłowska said we need the pressure of quotas to set an example that we're doing this. you mean it? push employers to make it harder for them? and if there are no disabled people, how do we then look for them in our committees and how do we employ them? i think we need to change our approach.
in writing a society that respects the dignity of every person as an absolute value should not be satisfied with the short-cut solution of quotas when promoting the inclusion of people with disabilities. they have only a short-term effect, and at the same time they call into question the fundamental principle of social inclusion, because they divide society. so let us stop talking about quotas and focus on measures that will have a long-term effect. inclusion must start in the school age so that all children, without distinction, have an equal opportunity to start developing their talents and skills which they can later apply in their job search. and instead of quotas, a transparent methodology and decision-making, complemented by a binding non-discriminatory job definition, is needed for the selection of staff. people with disabilities do not need a quota barrier, but a long-term solution that does not compromise their competence, hard work and commitment.
the essence of our common european market is the free movement of people and goods across the member states of the european union. not all countries have been fortunate in the past to have economic progress that allows them to pay wages at the level of germany, for example. small hauliers from slovakia, but also from other neighbouring countries, have successfully established themselves on european markets over the last ten years. in doing so, they increase employment in their countries and contribute to the growth of the european union as a whole. so let's not take away their earnings, let's not raise costs, let's not create unnecessary barriers. let's not build another iron curtain between east and west, this time commercial. the german legislation is a precedent in that it introduces a wage for employees from other countries. i am a strong supporter of the principle of free movement in our common european market, and that is why i am calling on the european commission to act in this case and to stop the german restrictions which are hurting citizens.

in writing. ‒ the the objective of the convention of the international maritime organisation on standards of training, qualification and watchkeeping for the crew of fishing vessels is to ensure that the personnel on board fishing vessels (mandatory only for vessels of 24 metres in length and over and of 750 kw and over) are qualified to demonstrate this qualification by an official certificate and to demonstrate their fitness for work by a medical examination. this would minimise the potential risk to life and property as well as the risk to the marine environment during operations on board vessels. as the european union cannot ratify the convention, it must be acceded to by the individual member states in accordance with the precedent in the tfeu concerning external competence, but the member states cannot ratify this convention without the authorisation of the european union. the purpose of this decision is to allow the member states to ratify that convention.

in writing. fraud harming the eu's financial interests costs the eu around eur 500 million a year, according to the rapporteur, and there are strong reasons to believe that up to eur 3 billion a year could be at risk from fraud. i think these are arguments which are sufficiently telling that we have to deal with them once and for all within the eu. i am convinced that the establishment of the european public prosecutor's office creates a new, more effective dimension for the fight against criminals suspected of fraud and criminal activity. i would also like to commend the establishment of this institution because it will serve as a bridge between the criminal justice systems of the member states, whose powers end at national borders, and the union institutions, which cannot prosecute. i also voted in favour of the report because the establishment of the european public prosecutor's office fills a gap in the legislation which has so far allowed some criminals to go unpunished for unlawfully evading taxpayers. the european parliament and the council will be consulted on the draft legislative proposal.
in writing. ‒ i support the establishment of a european public prosecutor's office to investigate and prosecute fraud involving eu funds. it is important to create a single and independent authority at european level and to step up prosecution in order to improve recovery and increase taxpayers' trust in the european institutions. at the same time, i would like to stress that the powers of the eppo should not be extended and should only concern european money.

for the ecr group commissioner mimica, the european union already gives 0.42% of its gross national income to development aid. this is significantly more than other oecd countries, which give only 0.28%. i do not know who decided that 0.7% is the ideal level for development aid, but it is clear that at a time when the european union is drowning in debt, when member states have tens of billions of invoices to pay, such a target is completely out of reach. moreover, development aid is in many cases just a transfer of money from poor people in rich countries to rich people in poor countries. in 2012, only 46% of development aid actually ended up in poor countries. not to mention waste, like in the congo, where more than half the projects have failed. so it's time to stop playing the big donor and stop having goals that are just unrealistic.
